WEB RESEARCH RESULT:
## 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported event/value

`javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory` is a JSSE provider-based engine class that creates `TrustManager` instances from trust material. That material may be supplied as a `KeyStore` or through provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`. The factory must be initialized before `getTrustManagers()` is called. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

The reported wording refers to the call event:

```text
TrustManagerFactory.init(KeyStore ks)
```

with the value `ks == null`. The Java API explicitly documents the `ks` parameter as “the key store, or null”; therefore, passing null is a supported API value, not an API-contract violation by itself. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

For the **SunJSSE** `PKIX` and `SunX509` implementations specifically, Oracle documents that a null `KeyStore` triggers default-trust-material discovery: first `javax.net.ssl.trustStore`, then `java-home/lib/security/jssecacerts`, then `java-home/lib/security/cacerts`; certain absent/misconfigured cases result in an empty keystore/default trust manager. This is reference-implementation/provider behavior, not a portable semantic guaranteed for every `TrustManagerFactory` provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

The phrase **“whose loading was not observed” is not language from the Java API documentation**. The API docs do say that an explicitly obtained `KeyStore` generally must be loaded before it can be accessed, except where it was already loaded during construction. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

More importantly, the supplied CrySL rule source does **not** contain `null`, `trustStore`, `cacerts`, `jssecacerts`, or `load`. It declares requirements named `generatedKeyStore[keyStore]` and `generatedManagerFactoryParameters[params]`; the meaning of those predicates and the detector’s “not observed” rendering are not defined by that rule file. Therefore, the supplied rule source alone cannot establish that the reported message means a Java `KeyStore.load(...)` call was required or missing.

## 2. Documented usage and any documented remediation

### Documented usage

* `TrustManagerFactory` is created with an algorithm name, optionally with an explicitly named provider or `Provider` object. Its purpose is to produce one or more trust managers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))
* Java SE 25 requires every Java-platform implementation to support the standard `PKIX` `TrustManagerFactory` algorithm. The standard-name specification describes it as producing `X509ExtendedTrustManager` objects that validate certificate chains under PKIX rules and requiring support for `CertPathTrustManagerParameters` initialization. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))
* A factory should be initialized using the initialization form appropriate to its provider: `init(KeyStore)` when a keystore supplies the trust material, or `init(ManagerFactoryParameters)` when the provider requires provider-specific parameters. Oracle’s JSSE guide explicitly says to consult the provider vendor if the appropriate initialization method is uncertain. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
* Calling `getTrustManagers()` before initialization results in `IllegalStateException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))
* For a general-purpose application, Oracle’s provider documentation recommends requesting a cryptographic service without pinning a named provider, because a named provider may not exist on other Java implementations and prevents use of a higher-preference implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

### Null `KeyStore` is not documented as misuse

There is **no official Java API recommendation to remediate a null `KeyStore` merely because it is null**. The API permits it, and the SunJSSE guide documents its default trust-material search behavior. Consequently, the official sources do not characterize this usage as unsafe or prescribe replacement with a particular keystore-loading sequence. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

If an application intentionally supplies explicit trust material, the documented API route is an initialized `KeyStore`; the `KeyStore` API says that a keystore must be loaded before access unless it was already loaded as part of instantiation. That is general API usage documentation, not a prescribed remediation for null initialization. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

### `SunX509`

Oracle’s JDK 25 provider documentation describes `SunX509` as a SunJSSE algorithm retained for backward compatibility and says it “should no longer be used.” It also documents different capabilities: SunJSSE `PKIX` supports initialization with either a `KeyStore` or `CertPathTrustManagerParameters`, whereas SunX509 supports a `KeyStore` but not `ManagerFactoryParameters`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

## 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and migration

| Topic | What the reviewed sources document |
|---|---|
| **Persisted formats** | `TrustManagerFactory` itself does not define a persisted format. `KeyStore` documentation says whether keystores are persistent, and their persistence mechanisms, are unspecified; multiple mechanisms and formats may exist. The sources provide no automatic truststore-format migration procedure for changing `TrustManagerFactory` initialization or algorithm. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html)) |
| **Wire formats / TLS protocol negotiation** | The reviewed `TrustManagerFactory` sources describe trust-manager construction and certificate-trust decisions, not TLS wire encoding or enabled/negotiated protocol versions. `SSLContext` is the separate API representing a secure-socket protocol implementation. No reviewed source states that changing this factory’s initialization mode changes a TLS protocol version or negotiated protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) |
| **Java-platform support** | `TrustManagerFactory` has existed since Java 1.4. In the reviewed Java SE 25 API, `PKIX` is required on every Java-platform implementation. Other algorithms depend on the installed provider and implementation release documentation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html)) |
| **Provider portability** | Provider choice and provider-specific algorithms are not portable by default. Oracle recommends not pinning a provider in general-purpose applications. The documented SunJSSE behavior for null `KeyStore` does not establish behavior for non-SunJSSE providers or non-JDK Java runtimes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html)) |
| **Migration path** | No reviewed official source specifies a migration procedure, compatibility guarantee, or equivalence guarantee for moving from `SunX509`, a default/null truststore selection, or a provider-specific factory to another configuration. Oracle documents that SunX509 should no longer be used, but does not give a step-by-step migration path in the reviewed material. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html)) |

In particular, neither `TrustManagerFactory.getInstance("TLS")` nor TLS protocol selection is involved here: `TrustManagerFactory` takes a **trust-management algorithm**, whereas `SSLContext` takes a secure-socket **protocol** identifier. The supplied finding and rule do not document an enabled or negotiated TLS protocol.

## 4. Exact matching rule in the supplied CrySL source

The source declares the governed specification type as `javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory`. Its event patterns name:

* `getInstance(algorithm)` and `getInstance(algorithm, _)`;
* `init(keyStore)` and `init(params)`;
* `trustManager = getTrustManagers()`.

The source therefore constrains the parameter-list shapes it declares:

* one or two arguments for `getInstance`; the second argument in the two-argument form is `_`, with no further textual constraint in this file;
* exactly one argument for either `init` form, tied to the declared `KeyStore` or `ManagerFactoryParameters` object variable;
* zero arguments, with an assigned return value, for `getTrustManagers`.

The exact matching and ordering clauses are:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(keyStore);
	i2: init(params);
	Init := i1 | i2;

	gtm1: trustManager = getTrustManagers();
	GetTrustMng := gtm1;

ORDER
	Get, Init, GetTrustMng?
```

The source’s explicit `CONSTRAINTS` condition is:

```text
algorithm in {"PKIX", "SunX509"};
```

It also declares the following requirements and postconditions:

```text
REQUIRES
	generatedKeyStore[keyStore];
	generatedManagerFactoryParameters[params];

ENSURES
	generatedTrustManager[this] after Init;
	generatedTrustManagers[trustManager] after GetTrustMng;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))

**Namesake methods:** based on the rule text itself, it is a specification for `javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory`, not a global name-only rule for all methods called `getInstance`, `init`, or `getTrustManagers`. Thus, a method that merely shares one of those names but is not the governed API type is not identified by this source as a match. The source does not state the analyzer’s detailed type-resolution behavior for inheritance, aliases, reflection, generated code, or unresolved calls; those remain unresolved.

**Rule/message limitation:** the exact CrySL source’s only literal algorithm constraint is the two-value allowlist `{"PKIX", "SunX509"}`. It does not literally express a null-`KeyStore` prohibition, default truststore lookup, or a `KeyStore.load` requirement. Any mapping from its symbolic `generatedKeyStore[...]` predicate to the detector message requires detector semantics outside this file.


**Source limitations:** This brief reviewed Oracle Java SE 25 documentation and the referenced CrySL file at the mutable `refs/heads/master` location. It did not verify the detector’s compiled rule artifact, the stated SHA-256 value, its predicate semantics, or the target runtime/provider. The SunJSSE null-keystore lookup sequence must not be generalized to all JSSE providers or platforms.
